title: Calgary police officer charged with two counts of murder in 2023 shooting
article: A Calgary police officer has been charged with two counts of second-degree murder after Alberta's oversight agency investigated a 2023 shooting that killed two men.

Constable Craig Stothard appeared in court Tuesday and was released, according to the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, or ASIRT, in a statement published later in the day. His bail was set for $1,000, and he must remain in the province under a curfew from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., with his passport surrendered.

The officer has been placed on leave, Calgary Police Service Chief Katie McLellan said in a separate statement. She declined to say whether his leave was with or without pay. He is a 15-year member of the service.

ASIRT said Constable Stothard allegedly shot two men driving in a van on May 29, 2023, on Memorial Drive in Calgary, a major thoroughfare. The police watchdog described the shooting as having happened after "a slow speed pursuit." The men were pronounced dead at the scene.
Court documents show that Wesley Davidson, 46, and Levon Boyce Fox, 39, were the men killed in the shooting. Police have not said which of the two men was driving the van.
A third man - Mr. Fox's brother, Dennis Wildman, 44 - was also in the vehicle but survived, said their mother, Lena Wildman, in an interview late Tuesday.

According to a Calgary police news release in 2023, the third person involved in the shooting, whom authorities did not identify, was taken into custody. That was her older son, Ms. Wildman confirmed. He was not charged in the incident, and Constable Stothard is not facing any charges connected with the injuries sustained by Mr. Wildman.
Mr. Fox's family belongs to the Goodstoney First Nation of the Stoney Nakoda people, located in southern Alberta.
"Things like this happen far too many times to Indigenous folks in this country," Ms. Wildman told The Globe and Mail. "Too many of us are killed by those who are supposed to protect us."
Constable Stothard's lawyer, Don MacLeod, said in a statement Tuesday that his client maintains his innocence. The officer "intends to mount a full and vigorous defence," Mr. MacLeod wrote.

On the day of the shooting, Calgary police had said that the incident occurred around 10:15 a.m. Officers had been called after hearing reports of an allegedly impaired driver "erratically" operating what police believe was a large stolen van. They said the driver was dangerous to the public.
Police claimed the shooting took place after the security guard of a private property became suspicious of three individuals.
"It is believed the individuals fled the scene in the five-ton van, colliding with a building and a barricade in the area as they sped away," the Calgary service wrote in a news release at the time.

Eventually, police located the van on Memorial Drive: "To prevent the van from entering the busy downtown core or neighbouring residential areas, multiple police units were called in to block intersections and bridges."
The vehicle, police claimed, made a sharp U-turn at an intersection, after which officers attempted to conduct a traffic stop that was unsuccessful.
"Despite the vehicle driving at low speeds at that time, the driver continued to swerve across all lanes of traffic and refused to stop," Calgary police said.

"Attempts were made to contain the vehicle. The van was able to break containment and continued moving towards officers, and at approximately 11 a.m., due to the rapidly changing dynamics, one officer, a 13-year member of the CPS, discharged their Service firearm."
Ms. Wildman said her sons had met Mr. Davidson for the first time on the day of the shooting. He had offered them a ride home.
"My younger son, who was living with me in Edmonton, had turned his life around," she said. "He was on his way to breaking away from his addictions to drugs, with medication and detox."
But Mr. Fox was worried about his older brother, she said: "He went to Calgary to see him because Dennis was really struggling with his addiction. They just wanted to come home."
Two members of Mr. Davidson's family on Tuesday declined to comment, requesting privacy. They have previously said that he also suffered from addiction issues.
Ms. Wildman said ASIRT spoke with her during its investigation.
"There is evidence that there is some racial motivation here," she said, speaking from her own perspective after her conversations with the police watchdog.

"But going forward, I'm not really confident about how this case would be handled, because we're talking about a member of police who did this. He should be treated like any other civilian, he just probably won't though."
On Tuesday, ASIRT said its investigation "provided reasonable grounds to believe that offences had been committed," allegedly by Constable Stothard.
Under the Police Act, the investigation was forwarded to Alberta Crown Prosecution Service, which reviewed the evidence and advised that it met the standard for prosecution.
Matthew Block, ASIRT's assistant executive director, determined that Constable Stothard should be charged with second-degree murder.
Mr. Block declined to provide any further details.
In a video statement posted online, Calgary Police Chief McLellan said the charges are extremely serious and that she is confident in the integrity of the investigation.

"We recognize that incidents like this challenge the trust that communities have in the Calgary Police Service, especially Indigenous communities," Chief McLellan said, extending her condolences to the family members of the two men.

She said Calgary police would not be providing any further comment on the case, as it is now before the courts: "Our criminal justice system is well equipped to handle this case with the seriousness and fairness it deserves."
Adam North Peigan, Mr. Fox's step-father, said that while the news stirred up sadness, he also finally felt a sense of relief after more than two years.
"There's been a lot of uncertainty, a lot of unanswered questions, a lot of anger, a lot of dealing with loss, mourning that loss," he said.
Mr. North Peigan said it would be "very hard on us as a family" if the officer does not plead guilty to the crimes.
"We've suffered years of oppression through colonization," he added. "That doesn't give, by no means, reason to shoot first and ask questions later."
With a report from Claire McFarlane
